summary: Defines a profile of the ACE framework that lets constrained servers hand off client authentication and authorization. It uses DTLS 1.2 or later for security between entities, with raw public keys or pre-shared keys. A resource-limited server can delegate authorization management to a trusted host with more capacity.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC describes how a small server can check who is allowed to do what without running a full authorization system. A separate authorization server hands the client a token and a secret, the client gives the token to the small server, and the two of them then open a secure DTLS channel that proves the token was really handed out to this client.

questions: what is the ace dtls profile
how does a constrained device check authorization
raw public key vs pre shared key in dtls
subtitle: How a tiny device and a client use DTLS and access tokens to decide who may access what.

tldr.problem: A resource-constrained server has little memory and no room for a full authorization system, but it still has to authenticate clients and decide what each one may do.
tldr.mechanism: The client gets an access token and the keying material from an authorization server, uploads the token to the resource server, and then sets up a DTLS channel using a raw public key or a pre-shared key that the token is bound to. The resource server checks each request against the rules carried in that token.
tldr.outcome: The constrained server delegates the hard authorization decisions to a more capable trusted host, and only has to store one token per client key. The RFC is a Proposed Standard updated by RFC 9430.

today: RFC 9202 is a Proposed Standard published in August 2022. It has not been obsoleted, but it is updated by RFC 9430. It is the DTLS profile of the ACE framework, and the text points to DTLS 1.3 as a later version that can be used instead of DTLS 1.2.

sections.title: A DTLS Profile for ACE
sections.content:
This RFC defines a profile of the Authentication and Authorization for Constrained Environments (ACE) framework, RFC 9200. In the profile, a client (C) and a resource server (RS) talk to each other with the Constrained Application Protocol (CoAP) of RFC 7252 over DTLS 1.2. The text uses DTLS 1.2 terminology, but later versions such as DTLS 1.3 in RFC 9147 can be used instead.

The client obtains an access token bound to a key, the proof-of-possession (PoP) key, from an authorization server (AS), to prove that it is allowed to reach protected resources held by the resource server. The authorization server also gives both sides the keying material they need to open a DTLS session. The communication between the client and the authorization server may be protected with DTLS as well. The profile supports two ways of proving possession: raw public keys (RPKs) from RFC 7250 and pre-shared keys (PSKs) from RFC 4279.

ACE requires the client and the server to authenticate each other before any application data is exchanged, and DTLS does that when both ends can prove they hold the keying material. The authorization server helps on the server side by putting the keying material, or information about it, into the access token, which is then a proof-of-possession token. The token itself is a CBOR web token, as recommended by RFC 9200.
sections.plainLanguage: The framework is called ACE. This RFC is one way of using it: over a small, cheap secure channel called DTLS, with a token that says what the client may do.

sections.title: The Three Parties and the Message Flow
sections.content:
Three parties are involved. The client wants to reach a protected resource on the resource server, and the authorization server decides who may reach what.

To find out which authorization server is in charge, the client can send an initial unauthorized resource request to the resource server, which denies it and returns AS Request Creation Hints containing the address of its authorization server. The client then asks that server for an access token at its token endpoint. Because the request and the response may carry confidential data, the client and the authorization server must protect that conversation, and the client is expected to be registered with the authorization server already.

Once the client holds the token, it can use it to open a DTLS session with the resource server. When the client will use an asymmetric proof-of-possession key, it must first upload the token to the authz-info endpoint on the resource server. With a symmetric key the same upload may be used, or the token may instead travel in the DTLS ClientKeyExchange message. In any case the DTLS mode must give replay protection.
sections.plainLanguage: The client asks the resource server which authorization server to talk to, gets a token from that server, hands the token to the resource server, and then opens the secure channel.

sections.title: Raw Public Key Mode
sections.content:
In raw public key mode, the client proves that it can use the public key that the token is bound to, and the server shows that it can use a public key of its own. The client sends a token request to the authorization server that carries a req_cnf object with either the raw public key or a unique identifier for a key the authorization server already knows. It is recommended that the client protect the request with DTLS using the same keying material, which proves possession of the key as part of the request.

The authorization server must check that the client it is talking to is the one associated with that key, and the access token must be bound to the client's public key through the cnf claim. The response names the profile to use, with the value coap_dtls, and normally carries the resource server's public key in the rs_cnf parameter. The authorization server must protect the integrity of the token, and its confidentiality as well if the token holds confidential data.

Before the handshake, the client uploads the token to the authz-info resource and waits for confirmation. The resource server then checks that the token is still valid, that it was meant for it, and that it came from an authorized authorization server. The handshake only finishes if both sides can use their own keying material. An implementation in this mode must support the cipher suite TLS_ECDHE_ECDSA_WITH_AES_128_CCM_8 and must implement support for the curve curve25519.
sections.plainLanguage: The client proves it holds a private key, and the token says which public key that is. The handshake only completes if both the client and the server can use the keys the token names.

sections.title: Pre-Shared Key Mode
sections.content:
In pre-shared key mode, the client and the resource server both prove that they hold the same symmetric secret, and the token is bound to that secret. The client may name a key identifier in the request. The authorization server must check that the identifier refers to a symmetric key it generated earlier for this client and this resource server, and if there is none it must generate a new one and return it.

The token carries a cnf claim with a COSE_Key object that holds either the shared secret itself or a key identifier. If the secret itself is in the token, the token must be encrypted with a COSE_Encrypt0 structure, using the keying material shared with the resource server. If only an identifier is in the token, the resource server derives the secret from a key derivation key that it shares with the authorization server, using a key derivation function. The RFC gives one example: HKDF with an empty salt, the key derivation key as the input keying material, and an info string that names the type, the length of the key and the access token.

The client uses the shared secret as a DTLS pre-shared key. It can either upload the token first and then name the key identifier in the psk_identity field, or put the most recent token itself in the psk_identity field of the ClientKeyExchange message. A client in this mode must support the cipher suite TLS_PSK_WITH_AES_128_CCM_8.
sections.plainLanguage: Both ends share a secret, and the token says which one. The server can work out the secret from the token alone, so the client and the server never have to exchange it again.

sections.title: Resource Access and Authorization Checks
sections.content:
Once the DTLS channel is up, the client may use the resources that the uploaded token covers. Every request that arrives on the channel has to be checked against the authorization rules that the token carries, and the server must check that the token is still valid for every request. An expired token must be removed.

A request must not be treated as authorized if any of five things fails: the message did not arrive on a secure channel set up by this procedure, the authorization information tied to the client is not valid, the request is not destined for this resource server, the resource named in the request is not covered by the authorization information, or the request method is not an authorized action on that resource. A request that arrives without any token tied to the client must be rejected with 4.01.

A request that arrives on a secure channel but is not authorized must be rejected with 4.03 when the resource is not covered by the authorization information, and with 4.05 when the resource is covered but the requested action is not allowed. Unauthorized requests over a DTLS session should be treated as non-fatal, so that the session stays alive until the token expires.
sections.plainLanguage: Every request is checked against the token: is the token still valid, is this the right server, does the token cover this resource, and does it allow this action.

sections.title: Updating Permissions and Expiring Tokens
sections.content:
The permissions on an established session can be changed without a new handshake. A resource server may only use a new access token for a session if the keying material bound to that token is the same one used in the DTLS handshake. Because the tokens are associated with the identifier of an existing session, the authorization information can be updated while the cryptographic keys stay as they are.

The client asks the authorization server for a new token, naming in the kid parameter the key identifier of the proof-of-possession key used for the existing channel. The authorization server must check that the identifier really is a valid verifier for a token it issued before, and decline the request with the error unsupported_pop_key otherwise. The new token must carry the same kid, and the resource server must replace the authorization information of the session identified by that key identifier.

Tokens that are no longer valid must be deleted. Because a DTLS association is always tied to specific tokens, a resource server must terminate an association once the last token bound to it has expired, and must first notify the client with a 4.01 error response for any long-running request.
sections.plainLanguage: A client can get new permissions during the same secure session, as long as it uses the same key. When the last token for a session expires, the server ends the session.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The authorization server must be sure that the keying material it hands to the resource server really belongs to the client. A malicious client could hand its own access token to somebody else. In raw public key mode the client should not be able to ask for a token for an arbitrary public key, because a token for a key whose private key the client cannot use allows an identity misbinding attack, in which the token can be used by somebody other than the intended client.

With pre-shared keys the security level depends on how random the keys are and on the cipher suite. Because the target is a constrained environment, the profile requires the same 8-byte tag cipher suites that CoAP mandates, while noting that 16-byte tags are preferable when the data volume makes them cheap. The RFC also warns that constrained devices running DTLS are open to denial of service, because the handshake creates state in the device, and that an unprotected authz-info endpoint lets an attacker fill a small server's storage with valid tokens, so the server should set a time limit for deleting tokens that have never been used.

Session resumption is treated with care: resuming would let a client skip proving possession of the proof-of-possession key again, so it should only be used with reasonably short-lived keys. The protection of stored tokens depends on the keying material between the authorization server and the resource server, and the server must process only tokens that are integrity protected and encrypted by an authorization server that is allowed to issue them for it.
sections.plainLanguage: The authorization server has to be sure the key it hands out belongs to the client, and small servers need protection from floods of tokens and from handshakes that cost them memory.

sections.title: Privacy Considerations
sections.content:
An unprotected response to an unauthorized request can reveal information about the resource server and about the relationship it has with the client, so an unencrypted answer should carry as little as possible. When a DTLS session already exists between an authenticated client and the server, a more detailed error response may be sent, because the client is known.

Unprotected requests can also reveal what the client is trying to reach and what it wants to send, so a client should not put confidential data in an unprotected request. Some information still leaks after the session is established, through the size of the messages and the source and destination addresses.
sections.plainLanguage: Error answers to clients that are not yet authenticated can leak information about the server, and requests sent before the channel is secure can leak what the client is doing.

viz.caption: The CoAP response codes this profile uses

items.label: Created
items.desc: The authorization server returns the access token.

items.label: Bad Request
items.desc: The token request is declined, for example for invalid parameters.

items.label: Unauthorized
items.desc: No token is tied to the client, or the token has expired.

items.label: Forbidden
items.desc: The token does not cover the resource named in the request.

items.label: Method Not Allowed
items.desc: The token covers the resource but not the requested action.

viz.caption: What the access token has to carry

items.title: A bound key
items.text: The proof-of-possession key that the client must be able to use.

items.title: An audience
items.text: The resource server the token is meant for.

items.title: A lifetime
items.text: When the token expires, checked on every request.

items.title: A profile name
items.text: coap_dtls, telling the client which profile to use.

items.title: The server's key
items.text: The resource server's public key, sent to the client in rs_cnf.
